Participants aged 13-15 years were recruited through schools, drug services, social media, posters and word-of-mouth.

Results: 175 participants completed the survey (Mage = 14.35, 54.9% female) and n=13 (7.4%) reported lifetime cannabis use. 16 participants (Mage=14.56, 75.0% female) completed the qualitative interview study, including 11 lifetime cannabis users.

We recruited nearly 200 13-15-year-old adolescent participants, including those who used cannabis, collected rich data about illegal cannabis use and mental health using indepth surveys and interviews, while keeping participants safe.

Most existing literature has either reported data from older cohorts when participants were adolescents in the early 2000s (Hines et al., 2023; Lees Thorne et al., 2025) or combined all illegal drugs without separately reporting cannabis use (Thornton et al., 2026; Ward et al., 2026).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Most existing literature has either reported data from older cohorts when participants were adolescents in the early 2000s (Hines et al., 2023; Lees Thorne et al., 2025) or combined all illegal drugs without separately reporting cannabis use (Thornton et al., 2026; Ward et al., 2026).
Recruitment was defined by the number of participants we recruited who started the survey.
Cannabis-user recruitment was defined by the number of lifetime cannabis user participants we recruited who started the survey.
All participants are asked whether they have been offered cannabis.

All participants are asked how much they think smoking cannabis will harm them (No harm to a lot of harm, or don't know) and to what extent they think regular cannabis use will harm their mental health (No risk to great risk, or don't know) (Wadsworth & Hammond, 2019).
Participants completed three five-point multiple-choice questions assessing the frequency, quantity, and frequency of heavy alcohol consumption during the past year.
Participants were encouraged to do the survey on a laptop or computer, but could do it on a smartphone if required.

One cannabis-using participant did not receive the CUDIT-R. 33 participants were not asked about: being offered cannabis, ease of getting cannabis and normality of cannabis questions, due to receiving an earlier version of the survey being used.
Four participants completed the qualitative study as well as the quantitative survey.
Most participants were recruited from school assemblies (n=143, 81.7%), with a minority being recruited through other routes (Figure 1).
Four participants said they had only used cannabis once, with three stating their total cannabis use days were between 2-5.
Four participants also reported total use days higher than 100.
One was elevated to level 3 because the participant had exceeded all scales' thresholds except drug use.
All participants were recruited from traceable sources.
Nine participants are current cannabis users and two used cannabis frequently in the past year.
Most long-term effects disclosed by participants were negative.

Despite this challenge, we recruited 175 adolescents to the quantitative study and 16 for qualitative interviews within a limited time window, with 13 lifetime and 11 frequent cannabis users, respectively.

This percentage falls within the 2023 SDD nationally representative data, which reports a rate of 7.1% lifetime cannabis use for 14-year-olds and 16.9% for 15-year-olds (NHS Digital, 2024), suggesting our recruitment efforts were able to reach early adolescent cannabis users, and tentatively suggests participants were being honest.
We recruited 11 frequent cannabis users in our qualitative study, with a current average frequency of 3 days/week and an average age of cannabis use onset of just over 13 years.
We deeply appreciate our participants' and parents' efforts, support, and engagement throughout the study.

text.text: Background: Approximately 10% of early adolescents in the UK report lifetime cannabis use.
However, contemporary UK research in this population remains limited due to recruitment, consent and safeguarding challenges.
We explored the feasibility of conducting research about cannabis use in UK adolescents aged 13-15 years.
Methods: This exploratory feasibility project comprised an online quantitative survey and qualitative interviews on cannabis use and mental health.
Participants aged 13-15 years were recruited through schools, drug services, social media, posters and word-of-mouth.
Participants consented through either a standard parent-and-adolescent pathway or an independent Gillick-competent pathway.
Feasibility outcomes included total recruitment, cannabis-user recruitment, successful data collection, and the extent of safeguarding actions required.

Results: 175 participants completed the survey (Mage = 14.35, 54.9% female) and n=13 (7.4%) reported lifetime cannabis use. 16 participants (Mage=14.56, 75.0% female) completed the qualitative interview study, including 11 lifetime cannabis users.
Two and four cannabis-using participants used the Gillick-competent pathway in the quantitative and qualitative studies, respectively.
In the quantitative study, 38/175 participants (21.7%) triggered low-intensity signposting and one participant received additional safeguarding actions.
Three qualitative participants received safeguarding actions.
Both studies successfully elicited detailed information on cannabis use, mental health and contextual experiences.

We recruited nearly 200 13-15-year-old adolescent participants, including those who used cannabis, collected rich data about illegal cannabis use and mental health using indepth surveys and interviews, while keeping participants safe.
We therefore proved we can feasibly conduct research about cannabis in <16-year-olds in the UK.

text.text:  175 13-15-year-olds (Mage=14.35) completed a survey about illegal drug use and mental health, including 13 lifetime cannabis users.  16 13-15-year-olds (Mage=14.56) completed a qualitative interview study, including 11 lifetime cannabis users.

In one of the very few contemporary studies in the UK, we demonstrated that we can feasibly and ethically conduct quantitative survey and qualitative interview research about cannabis with 13-15-year-olds.
Cannabis is the most widely used illicit drug among school-aged adolescents in the UK.
In England, 7% of adolescents aged 11-15 years have used cannabis during their lifetime, and 8% of 15-year-olds have used cannabis in the past month (NHS Digital, 2024).
text.formatted: In England, 7% of adolescents aged 11-15 years have used cannabis during their lifetime, and 8% of 15-year-olds have used cannabis in the past month <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(NHS Digital, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In Scotland and Wales, 19% of 15-year-olds/Year 11 students have used cannabis at least once (Inchley et al., 2023; Page et al., 2023).

text.text: Of lifetime cannabis users in the UK, survey results suggest that about one-third first tried cannabis before the age of 15 (Spinazzola et al., 2025).

text.text: However, in the UK, contemporary research about cannabis in under-16-year-olds is extremely limited.

Consuming cannabis frequently carries psychiatric risks, including an increased risk of psychotic disorder (Marconi et al., 2016) and a small but increased risk of mood disorders (Lev-Ran et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Consuming cannabis frequently carries psychiatric risks, including an increased risk of psychotic disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Marconi et al., 2016)</ref> and a small but increased risk of mood disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lev-Ran et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Earlier initiation of cannabis use is specifically associated with a greater chance of psychotic disorder (McDonald et al., 2024), cannabis use disorder (Lawn et al., 2022) and later substance abuse (Lynskey et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Earlier initiation of cannabis use is specifically associated with a greater chance of psychotic disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(McDonald et al., 2024)</ref>, cannabis use disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Lawn et al., 2022)</ref> and later substance abuse <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Lynskey et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: In England, among the 16,212 under-18-year-olds who received formal support at a drug and alcohol service between 2024 and 2025, 71% of them received this support because of cannabis, and around 50% of these cannabis-using service users were under the age of 16 (Office for Health Improvement and Disparities [OHID], 2025).
text.formatted: In England, among the 16,212 under-18-year-olds who received formal support at a drug and alcohol service between 2024 and 2025, 71% of them received this support because of cannabis, and around 50% of these cannabis-using service users were under the age of 16 (Office for Health Improvement and Disparities <ref type="bibr">[OHID], 2025)</ref>.

text.text: While national survey statistics in the UK repeatedly demonstrate that a non-negligible proportion of early adolescents are using cannabis (NHS Digital, 2024; Public Health Wales, 2026), contemporary British academic research providing details on cannabis use in <16year-olds remains sparse.

text.text: Most existing literature has either reported data from older cohorts when participants were adolescents in the early 2000s (Hines et al., 2023; Lees Thorne et al., 2025) or combined all illegal drugs without separately reporting cannabis use (Thornton et al., 2026; Ward et al., 2026).

text.text: There are some exceptions, however; Page et al. (2021) reported an increase in past-month cannabis use in Wales through a national school survey of 11-16-year-olds in Wales.

text.text: While Hotham et al. (2023) and Hines et al. (2024) reported associations between type of cannabis use and mental health outcomes, they used data from a whole-school, all-substance use prevention trial.

text.text: Due to their broader focus, these studies lack detail on cannabis use behaviour and details. Humphreys et al. (2025) investigated cannabis experiences and motives in 55 students aged 13-16 years in an alternative provision (AP) school using online surveys.

(2025)</ref> investigated cannabis experiences and motives in 55 students aged 13-16 years in an alternative provision (AP) school using online surveys.

text.text: This appears to be the only contemporary study that specifically set out to investigate early adolescent cannabis use and offers rich insight into cannabis use in a younger age group in the UK.
In short, only a handful of academic papers have studied cannabis use in under-16s over the past 20 years in the UK, and most involved analysis of large-scale existing datasets.
This usually limits the cannabis-related detail available, as well as avoiding major ethical and safeguarding responsibilities of the researcher collecting data.
We believe that given the size of the early adolescent cannabis user population in the UK, this group deserves dedicated, detailed research attention.
Internationally, more recent research has investigated under-16 cannabis use (Ashdown-Franks et al., 2019; Son et al., 2025; Smith et al., 2019; Forman-Hoffman et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Internationally, more recent research has investigated under-16 cannabis use <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ashdown-Franks et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Son et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Smith et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Forman-Hoffman et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative studies that gain rich data in younger age-groups also exist in US, Canada and Norway (Jenkins et al., 2017; Haines-Saah et al., 2014; Friese, 2017; Bilgrei et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Qualitative studies that gain rich data in younger age-groups also exist in US, Canada and Norway <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Jenkins et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Haines-Saah et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Friese, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bilgrei et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, most papers report findings from large health-general surveys or include mixed age ranges, including those over 16.
Thus, there appears to be limited international research that specifically investigates cannabis and focuses on under-16s.

We believe there is particular need for cannabis-oriented research in under-16s, given this is when cannabis use often begins and the heightened harms of an earlier onset of cannabis use (Hosseini & Oremus, 2019).
text.formatted: We believe there is particular need for cannabis-oriented research in under-16s, given this is when cannabis use often begins and the heightened harms of an earlier onset of cannabis use <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hosseini & Oremus, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This lack of detailed cannabis research into early adolescents may reflect the unique challenge of researching illegal drug use among <16-year-olds.
text.formatted: This lack of detailed cannabis research into early adolescents may reflect the unique challenge of researching illegal drug use among <16-year-olds.

text.text: Potential participants may worry that their disclosures of illegal drug use are told to caring adults, which reduces willingness to participate and compromises honesty of answers (Berlan & Bravender, 2009; Fisher, 2003).
text.formatted: Potential participants may worry that their disclosures of illegal drug use are told to caring adults, which reduces willingness to participate and compromises honesty of answers <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Berlan & Bravender, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Fisher, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Full confidentiality can never be guaranteed due to the moral and legal obligation to protect <16-year-old adolescents when they are at risk of serious harm (Children Act, 1989).
text.formatted: Full confidentiality can never be guaranteed due to the moral and legal obligation to protect <16-year-old adolescents when they are at risk of serious harm <ref type="bibr">(Children Act, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Good practice is to carefully and candidly explain to adolescents how sensitive disclosures will be handled, as in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study in the US (Clark et al., 2018; Clark et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Good practice is to carefully and candidly explain to adolescents how sensitive disclosures will be handled, as in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study in the US <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clark et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Clark et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, given the complexity and ambiguity of safeguarding timing, effectively teaching younger participants these confidentialitybreaking rules can be difficult.
Therefore, deciding when to break confidentiality and how to safeguard, versus maintaining confidentiality, in early adolescent research studies is challenging (Hiriscau et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Therefore, deciding when to break confidentiality and how to safeguard, versus maintaining confidentiality, in early adolescent research studies is challenging <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hiriscau et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This is often referred to as 'Gillick competence' (Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech Area Health Authority, [1985]), although its application to observational non-medical research is not a formal, legal term.

text.text: These policies have been used by researchers who investigate vulnerable adolescent populations, for example, studies on LGBTQ+ populations (e.g. Todd, 2024; Cwinn et al., 2021 (Canada); Mustanski et al. (2017) (US)).

(2017)</ref> (US)).

text.text: However, in practice, British Research Ethics Committees (RECs) may default to requiring parental consent (Barker et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, in practice, British Research Ethics Committees (RECs) may default to requiring parental consent <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barker et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, most UK under-16 adolescent research utilises the parental consent with child assent approach, even though recruitment or data quality may be compromised by obligating the involvement of parents when studying a sensitive topic (Tigges, 2003; Rojas et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Consequently, most UK under-16 adolescent research utilises the parental consent with child assent approach, even though recruitment or data quality may be compromised by obligating the involvement of parents when studying a sensitive topic <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Tigges, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Rojas et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, parental opt-out consent procedures are often used in large survey studies (NHS Digital, 2024).
text.formatted: Alternatively, parental opt-out consent procedures are often used in large survey studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(NHS Digital, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers also meet recruitment challenges.
It is difficult to establish reliable routes to ethically and effectively invite early adolescents to participate in research, especially cannabis users.

Schools provide access to large numbers of early adolescents, but participation is constrained by time limits and awkwardness in publicly discussing topics like illegal drug use (Hatch et al., 2023; Tyler & Davies, 2013).
text.formatted: Schools provide access to large numbers of early adolescents, but participation is constrained by time limits and awkwardness in publicly discussing topics like illegal drug use <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hatch et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Tyler & Davies, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, despite caring for early adolescents who use drugs, researchers may find it hard to successfully recruit from healthcare and drug services due to time and clinical pressures (Loades et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Similarly, despite caring for early adolescents who use drugs, researchers may find it hard to successfully recruit from healthcare and drug services due to time and clinical pressures <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Loades et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: To summarise, cannabis use during early adolescence in the UK is not rare.
Many UK lifetime cannabis users try cannabis for the first time before 16, and initiating frequent use at an earlier age is predictive of worse outcomes (Hosseini & Oremus, 2019).
text.formatted: Many UK lifetime cannabis users try cannabis for the first time before 16, and initiating frequent use at an earlier age is predictive of worse outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hosseini & Oremus, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this, very little research has been published on early adolescent cannabis use, particularly contemporary research and research that specifically focuses on cannabis use behaviour.
This is likely due to ethical and logistical challenges.

Therefore, we evaluated the feasibility of conducting exploratory research into cannabis use among UK early adolescents through both a quantitative questionnaire study and a qualitative interview study about cannabis use and mental health.
The indicators of feasibility were: (i) recruitment, (ii) data collection success and (iii) extent of sign-posting and safeguarding actions required.
We report the strategies we undertook to achieve our goals, namely: our multi-route recruitment method, the independent Gillick-competent consent pathway, and a tiered safeguarding protocol.
Quantitative questionnaire data collection began in December 2024 and ended in July 2026, including two active data collection periods that cumulatively totalled approximately 10 months.
Qualitative data collection began in June 2024 and ended in July 2026, including two active data collection periods that cumulatively totalled 5 months.
Participants could provide their consent through two pathways.
First, through the standard combined parental consent and adolescent assent pathway.
Alternatively, the adolescent could consent via the Gillick-competent pathway (HRA, 2026).

In this approach, participants could consent independently after they passed an interview in which they proved they understood the aims, content, risks and benefits, confidentiality and safeguarding protocol of the study.

Competency interviews were run over the phone or via MS Teams and comprised questions to test whether they genuinely understood the study, and how confidentiality, signposting and the safeguarding process work.
This consenting process is based on the Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech Area Health Authority [1986] legal case.
text.formatted: This consenting process is based on the Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech Area Health Authority <ref type="bibr">[1986]</ref> legal case.

text.text: All participants received default, generic signposting to substance use and mental health services in the information sheet.

We then informed participants in advance of participation about when confidentiality would be broken, what safeguarding action would be taken, and what information could or could not be shared with others.
This signposting and safeguarding protocol was informed by Clark et al.'s (2018) approach and received further input from clinicians, adolescent research academics, and a school safeguarding lead.
text.formatted: This signposting and safeguarding protocol was informed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Clark et al.'s (2018)</ref> approach and received further input from clinicians, adolescent research academics, and a school safeguarding lead.

text.text: The actions are based on qualitative disclosures or high quantitative questionnaire scores.
Table 1 shows the three levels of actions that were taken based on different conditions.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> shows the three levels of actions that were taken based on different conditions.

text.text: Quantitative study
The quantitative study was an online survey combining questionnaires about cannabis use, drug and mental health, and computerised cognitive tasks.
The survey was for 13-15-year-olds regardless of their past cannabis or drug use.
We evaluated recruitment, cannabis user recruitment, successful data collection, and safeguarding outcomes.
We collected descriptive findings on mental health and cannabis use outcomes.
Ethical approval was granted by King's College London REC, ID: 43622.
Recruitment.
The quantitative study was mainly advertised through voluntary school assemblies about cannabis presented by WL.
WL gave about 25 assemblies to about 4,000 secondary school students in 2024-2026.
The study was also advertised through physical posters, collaboration with drug services, paid advertisements on social media platforms (in 2024), and word of mouth.
We spent around £1,500 on Snapchat and TikTok advertisements in summer 2024.
Three drug services said they would help with recruitment.
Participants could join both quantitative and qualitative studies.
Feasibility outcomes.
Recruitment was defined by the number of participants we recruited who started the survey.
Cannabis-user recruitment was defined by the number of lifetime cannabis user participants we recruited who started the survey.
Successful data collection was defined by the proportion of people who started the survey and completed it, demonstrating acceptability of the survey to the participants.
Furthermore, successful data collection was assessed by preliminary descriptive results.
Safeguarding outcomes were defined as the number of participants requiring different levels of safeguarding actions.
Cannabis use was measured through standard questions assessing lifetime cannabis use, time since last use, lifetime cannabis use days, cannabis use initiation age and cannabis use frequency.

Cannabis users also reported their typical weights (in grams) of cannabis consumed on a day of use from 0.1 to 5+, the type of cannabis they commonly used (skunk, hash/resin, herbal/Thai/ditch-weed or other), the route of administration (vape, eat or smoke) and the location they used cannabis (home, school, friend's House or park) through multiple-choice questions.
Cannabis use was always kept confidential, regardless of extent, and did not trigger individualised signposting or safeguarding.
Cannabis users reported problematic cannabis use in the past 6 months through the CUDIT-R (Adamson et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Cannabis users reported problematic cannabis use in the past 6 months through the CUDIT-R <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adamson et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: It comprises 8 multiple-choice items on hazardous cannabis use and dependence symptoms, and each item is coded from 0 to 4.
The final score is the sum of all ratings.
Cannabis users reported past-year cannabis use motivation was measured using the adapted BCAMM (Bartel et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Cannabis users reported past-year cannabis use motivation was measured using the adapted BCAMM <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bartel et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: After adaptation, six 5-point Likertscale items each identify a specific reason for cannabis use.
Participants rated the frequency based on the extent to which their cannabis use was driven by these aims from 'never' to 'always' and were coded from 1 to 5.
All participants are asked whether they have been offered cannabis.
All participants reported how normal it is to use cannabis (Not at all to a lot, or don't know) and how easy it is to get cannabis (Very easy to very hard) in the UK.

All participants are asked how much they think smoking cannabis will harm them (No harm to a lot of harm, or don't know) and to what extent they think regular cannabis use will harm their mental health (No risk to great risk, or don't know) (Wadsworth & Hammond, 2019).
text.formatted: All participants are asked how much they think smoking cannabis will harm them (No harm to a lot of harm, or don't know) and to what extent they think regular cannabis use will harm their mental health (No risk to great risk, or don't know) <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Wadsworth & Hammond, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Drug use history other than cannabis was collected through a drug history questionnaire which assessed lifetime/yearly/monthly substance use including alcohol, tobacco, CBD, magic mushrooms, nitrous oxide/laughing gas, ketamine, cocaine, MDMA and E-cigarette.
For participants who report use in the last month, they are asked for the exact number of days that they used that substance.
Any participants who reported a frequency of using these drugs equal to or higher than 2 days/week were individually signposted.
Problematic alcohol use was assessed by AUDIT-C (Bush et al., 1998).
text.formatted: Problematic alcohol use was assessed by AUDIT-C <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bush et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Participants completed three five-point multiple-choice questions assessing the frequency, quantity, and frequency of heavy alcohol consumption during the past year.
Answers for each question were converted to ratings from 0-4, and the score is the sum.
Any participants who scored 5 or above were individually signposted.
Depression.
Depression in the past week was measured through the DASS-21 -depression subscale (Henry & Crawford, 2005).
text.formatted: Depression in the past week was measured through the DASS-21 -depression subscale <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Henry & Crawford, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: This subscale includes seven 4-point Likert-scale items, each ranging from 0 (Not apply at all) to 3 (Apply very much).
The score is two times the sum.
Any score of 21 or above was considered severe and were individually signposted.
Anxiety was measured through the GAD-7 (Spitzer et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Anxiety was measured through the GAD-7 <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Spitzer et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: GAD-7 comprises seven 4-point Likert-scale questions, each asking the perceived frequency of anxiety symptoms in the past 2 weeks from 0 (Not at all) to 3 (Nearly every day).
The anxiety score was the sum of all items, and any score of 15 or above was considered severe and were individually signposted.
Psychotic-like symptoms were measured through the CAPE-15 (Capra et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Psychotic-like symptoms were measured through the CAPE-15 <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Capra et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: CAPE-15 contains 15 4-point Likert scale items, measuring the frequency and the distress of positive psychotic-like symptoms over the past 3 months from 0 to 3.
The psychotic-like symptom score was the sum of all frequency items.
A score of 22 or above (average≥1.47) was considered severe (Bukenaite et al., 2017) and individually signposted.
text.formatted: A score of 22 or above (average≥1.47) was considered severe <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bukenaite et al., 2017)</ref> and individually signposted.

text.text: Other.
Demographics.
Demographic information included gender, age, sexual orientation, and ethnicity.

We also measured impulsivity, personality, cannabis self-identity, school engagement, and police interactions with questionnaires, and used cognitive task measures of working memory and response inhibition, but these are not reported in this manuscript.
Participants received an information sheet and were asked which consent route they preferred after contacting the research team.
Participants who wanted to consent independently underwent the Gillick competency interview.
After providing their consent, they received a Gorilla link to the survey.
Participants did the survey at home in their own time.
Participants were encouraged to do the survey on a laptop or computer, but could do it on a smartphone if required.
Participants first confirmed that they had not used cannabis in the preceding 12 hours and provided their consent again.
They then completed the survey.
Participants who reported lifetime cannabis use received extra questions on cannabis use details, cannabis use motives and problematic cannabis use.
The total time commitment is around 30-45 minutes.
Participants received a £20 Amazon voucher as compensation for their time.

Recruitment.
The recruitment method was the same as the quantitative survey study.
The only difference was that cannabis users were prioritised in the qualitative study.
Eligibility Criteria.

Inclusion criteria were: (i) aged 13-15 years, (ii) speak English, and (iii) either be a (1) current weekly cannabis user or recent weekly user, or (2) have never used cannabis but have been offered it.

The exclusion criteria are: 1) History of psychosis; 2) Suicidal thoughts or self-harm; 3) Previous use of heroin, crack cocaine or methamphetamine; 4) Unable to be interviewed for 1.5 hours, as judged by the participant, parent/carer, or researcher; and 5) Says that participation in the study will endanger them.

text.text: The topics covered during the interview are determined through discussions with clinicians, safeguarding leads, academics and through a review of existing literature.
The interview topic guide was written by co-authors, including an experienced qualitative researcher (ML).

Topics included: (i) reasons for cannabis initiation, (ii) reasons for continued use, (iii) perceived shortterm effects, (iv) perceived long-term effects, (v) context of cannabis use, (vi) knowledge of cannabis and (vii) the impact of cannabis use on their relationship with their family among cannabis users.

For non-users, the five main topics in the interview schedule were: (i) their experience with cannabis, (ii) reason for not using cannabis, (iii) harm perception of cannabis, (iv) thoughts on peers who use cannabis, and (v) policymaking around cannabis use.
Interviews were offered online or in person, conducted by a postgraduate researcher (LF or AS).
The interview was expected to take around 1 hour.
Interviews were audio-recorded with consent.
We collected demographics and cannabis use days per week before the interview.
After the interview, participants received a £20 Amazon voucher.

Reason for not using cannabis.
Reasons for not using cannabis varied, including avoiding harm, concern about parents' feelings, educational worries and violation of moral beliefs.
"I wanna live a longer life and like I don't want that to be like if someone found out or like school found out, that could just ruin me and what education that have."
Harm perception of cannabis.
Participants described potential harms such as executive function deficit, physical harms, mental health risks and addiction.
Thoughts on peers who use cannabis.
The attitudes toward peers who use cannabis are mixed.
Non-user participants showed sympathy, but they also reported negative thoughts and expressed a willingness to maintain distance.
"I do feel bad for them because obviously they could have better opportunities in their life."
Policy-making around cannabis use.
Most participants said cannabis should remain illegal in the UK.
For current cannabis users, they stressed the need for rehabilitation instead of punishment.
They suggested that sorting out the root cause of cannabis use and rehabilitation is crucial.
"People do weed should not be arrested for it.
They should like just be given help because if you're arrested for, I feel like you're recycling, you'll just end up receiving it in prison, or you'll just end up doing it again when you come out."

Participants with cannabis use experiences described reasons such as peer influences, coping mechanisms and family exposure.
"My mum's has been using weed for 20 years, so when I was really little, I would see her do it.
Like, and then we get to 13, my cousin, she did it.
A year later, she smoked 20 joints, yeah, and she'll leave them (joints) in the house.
I just took a couple of joints.
Then I just like, get off my cousin and just smoke it".
Reasons for continued use.
Several participants suggested they continued using cannabis because cannabis makes them feel relaxed and helps them cope with challenges.
Others attributed ongoing use to dependence.
"I started taking it more often whenever we go out, whenever we have breaks, whenever, just maybe we are at home alone…so that's how it turns like addiction and so on."
Short-term effects.
Participants noted both positive and negative short-term effects.
"I started laughing at things that weren't even there.
I just felt everything around me was really funny.
And later on, I started feeling sleepy and I had trouble concentrating."
Long-term effects.
Most long-term effects disclosed by participants were negative.
Notably, 3 participants suggested that they did not perceive any long-term effects.

While in other families, cannabis use had been normalised.

This study explored the feasibility of conducting research on cannabis use among early adolescents in the UK.
In spite of the sensitive nature of the research and ethical and logistical challenges, we successfully recruited 187 13-15-year-old participants, through a range of recruitment methods.
We recorded information from 13 lifetime cannabis users in our quantitative survey and 11 frequent cannabis users in our qualitative interview study.
We utilised a Gillick-competent independent consent pathway for some participants.
We collected data about illegal cannabis and other drug use, mental health and contextual cannabis-related factors.
We maintained full confidentiality about cannabis use, while safeguarding participants with a tiered safeguarding protocol relating to mental health and drug use.
Overall, our findings support the feasibility of specifically researching cannabis and other illegal drug use, in detail, among adolescents under 16 years old in the UK.

We demonstrated that we can gain ethical approvals to study illegal cannabis use in children in the UK and then demonstrated we can successfully collect quantitative and qualitative data on cannabis-related details in under-16s, including both cannabis users and non-users.
This is despite the fact that parental involvement negatively affects engagement (Rojas et al., 2008) and adolescents may lie about their cannabis use (Delaney-Black et al., 2010).

text.text: Beyond secondary analysis of existing survey data (Page et al., 2021) and baseline trial data (Hines et al., 2024; Hotham et al., 2023), our study is one of the few contemporary studies that investigate cannabis use in <16-year-olds in the UK.

text.text: This is a significant research achievement, given (i) the prevalence of early adolescent cannabis use and its impact on wellbeing, and (ii) the ethical and logistical challenges of conducting such research.

Early adolescents are hard to reach when considering the competing goals in recruitment sources (schools and health services), and cannabis users could be harder to reach due to confidentiality concerns.

Despite this challenge, we recruited 175 adolescents to the quantitative study and 16 for qualitative interviews within a limited time window, with 13 lifetime and 11 frequent cannabis users, respectively.

The quantitative sample size therefore supports using school assemblies to recruit participants for studies on sensitive topics and demonstrates the potential of social media and third-sector clinical services to enlarge sample size and recruit substance users.
Meanwhile, engagement from third-sector clinical services is sometimes inconsistent, suggesting that a major recruitment method (e.g., school assemblies) alongside clinical services is necessary.

It is notable that many parents or carers were willing for their child to participate in our research, specifically about cannabis use and mental health, even under the knowledge that they would not be informed about any cannabis use.
This demonstrates the feasibility of working with parents, and explaining that their child's cannabis use will not be disclosed to them, due to research confidentiality.
The Children Act 1989 obligates researchers to safeguard under-16s.
These duties offer protection but may also worry potential adolescent participants, especially those who use cannabis, that their answers will be told to adults to protect them (Fisher, 2003).

text.text: Nonetheless, cannabis users comprised 7.4% of our quantitative sample, with an average age of 14.3 years.

This percentage falls within the 2023 SDD nationally representative data, which reports a rate of 7.1% lifetime cannabis use for 14-year-olds and 16.9% for 15-year-olds (NHS Digital, 2024), suggesting our recruitment efforts were able to reach early adolescent cannabis users, and tentatively suggests participants were being honest.
We also proved that questionnaires and interviews were well accepted by early adolescents by finding a high completion rate, even when focusing on sensitive topics.
A potential explanation for participants' willingness to disclose their cannabis use could be our safeguarding strategy.
Built on Clark et al. (2018), we explain to participants in what condition confidentiality will be broken and describe different levels of safeguarding action in advance.

text.text: Cannabis use was never a reason to signpost or safeguard, regardless of frequency or intensity of use.
In this context, one in five participants crossed at least one mental-health or non-cannabis-drug-use threshold, and one in four disclosed events that required signposting or safeguarding actions.

This result stressed the necessity of planning a safeguarding protocol before data collection, but the proportion and the fact that we encountered no severe adverse events also showed the risk is manageable.
After we conducted corresponding safeguarding actions, we did not receive any complaints from participants.
In general, appropriate safeguarding is compatible with substantial and sensitive data collection within early adolescents.
Another factor supporting our recruitment of cannabis users can be the Gillick-competent consent pathway.

In past adolescent substance use research, it has been used mainly in substance use intervention studies (Deluca et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015), while its use in observational adolescent drug use studies is rare.

We believe RECs should be applauded for enabling this research, as other RECs should also be praised for enabling studies involving other sensitive topics like sexual orientation in LGBTQ+ child participants (Todd, 2024).

text.text: The quantitative data we collected provide preliminary insights into cannabis use profiles during early adolescence.

Quantitative data reveal kind of cannabis was consumed, where it was consumed, methods of administration, quantities consumed, motives for use, and other drug use, as well as illuminating norms and harm perceptions amongst non-users.
This demonstrates the value of a more detailed cannabis-and drug-focused survey.
We recruited 11 frequent cannabis users in our qualitative study, with a current average frequency of 3 days/week and an average age of cannabis use onset of just over 13 years.
This is a young and potentially vulnerable sample.

Within a reasonable, less-than-one-hour interview length, the qualitative interview provided contextual information about cannabis use initiation, environments, motives, personal experiences, and attitudes.
These findings illustrate the level of detail and nuance that can be feasibly collected from this age group.

For example, the frequent disclosure of difficult and drug-related experiences by users and experiences of being offered cannabis but rejecting it by non-users showed the kind of rich data we can receive from early adolescents.
Taken together, specialised research into early adolescents' drug use provided unique findings that went beyond binary or other simple measures offered by large epidemiological studies.
These studies show the promise that these research efforts have for uncovering important, undiscovered elements of early adolescent cannabis use.
Although we have preliminarily demonstrated feasibility, several limitations remain.
The number of participants who consented through the Gillick-competent pathway was small.

One explanation is that cannabis-using participants did not have to disclose their cannabis use to their parents because they did not have to be cannabis users to take part, which is a strength of the study design in the first place.
Nonetheless, the assessment of Gillick competence can be improved by ensuring participants understand this option from the start and reducing burden of the competency interview.
Another concern is our use of school assemblies to recruit, which were about the potential harms of cannabis use and were delivered by the principal investigator (WL).
We showed that we can approach many under-16s with cannabis use experience through school assemblies and it is a cost-effective way of reaching hundreds of teenagers.
However, it comes with the limitation of potentially biasing the students and potential participants into not disclosing cannabis use to the cannabis education expert, who is also the researcher.

Furthermore, past literature reported strong correlations between frequent cannabis use and truancy and exclusion from mainstream schools (McCrystal et al., 2005; McCrystal et al., 2007), although we did also advertise in alternative provision schools to address this issue.

text.text: Many under-16 early adolescents in the UK have used cannabis.
However, research about cannabis with this age group in the UK is extremely limited.
We prove we can feasibly recruit these participants and study cannabis use in detail, despite ethical and logistical challenges.
These findings provide a methodological basis for larger studies that investigate the onset, continuation, consequences, and treatment of cannabis use during early adolescence.
It also contributes to the growing literature on how to study sensitive topics among <16-year-old children.
